content: Dexamethasone is a corticosteroid that mimics a natural hormone produced by your adrenal glands. It is often prescribed to replace this hormone when your body does not produce enough of it. This medication is used to treat conditions such as inflammation, severe allergies, asthma, and certain types of cancer. It may also be prescribed for other uses, so consult your doctor or pharmacist for additional information. Dexamethasone is available as a tablet or an oral solution. Your doctor will provide a dosing schedule tailored to your needs. Follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully, and ask your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Take dexamethasone exactly as directed. Do not take more or less of it, or take it more frequently than prescribed. Do not stop taking dexamethasone without consulting your doctor, as abrupt discontinuation can lead to symptoms such as loss of appetite, upset stomach, vomiting, drowsiness, confusion, headache, fever, joint and muscle pain, peeling skin, and weight loss. If you have been on high doses for a prolonged period, your doctor will likely reduce your dose gradually to allow your body to adjust before stopping the medication completely. Monitor for these side effects during dose reduction and after stopping the medication, even if you switch to an inhaled form. If these symptoms occur, contact your doctor immediately. You may need to temporarily increase your dose or restart the medication. Before taking dexamethasone, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to dexamethasone, aspirin, tartrazine (a yellow dye found in some foods and drugs), or any other medications. Provide a list of all prescription and nonprescription medications you are taking, especially anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin), arthritis medications, aspirin, cyclosporine, digoxin, diuretics, ephedrine, estrogen, ketoconazole, oral contraceptives, phenobarbital, phenytoin, rifampin, theophylline, and vitamins. If you have a fungal infection (other than on your skin), consult your doctor before taking dexamethasone. Inform your doctor if you have or have ever had liver, kidney, intestinal, or heart disease; diabetes; an underactive thyroid; high blood pressure; mental illness; myasthenia gravis; osteoporosis; herpes eye infection; seizures; tuberculosis; or ulcers. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you become pregnant while taking dexamethasone, contact your doctor immediately. If you are undergoing surgery, including dental surgery, inform your doctor or dentist that you are taking dexamethasone. If you have a history of ulcers or take high doses of aspirin or arthritis medications, limit your alcohol consumption while on dexamethasone, as it increases the risk of stomach and intestinal irritation, which can lead to ulcers. Your doctor may recommend a specific diet, such as low-sodium, low-salt, potassium-rich, or high-protein. Follow these dietary instructions. Dexamethasone may cause stomach upset, so take it with food or milk. If you miss a dose, ask your doctor what to do. Write down these instructions for future reference. If you take dexamethasone once daily, take the missed dose as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one. Dexamethasone may cause side effects. Notify your doctor if you experience any of the following symptoms, especially if they are severe or persistent: upset stomach, stomach irritation, vomiting, headache, dizziness, insomnia, restlessness, depression, anxiety, acne, increased hair growth, easy bruising, or irregular/absent menstrual periods. If you experience serious side effects such as a skin rash, swelling of the face, lower legs, or ankles, vision problems, prolonged infections, muscle weakness, or black/tarry stools, contact your doctor immediately. Serious side effects can be reported to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program. Store dexamethasone in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excess heat and moisture (not in the bathroom). Dispose of expired or unneeded medication properly. Consult your pharmacist for disposal instructions. In case of overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual collapses or is not breathing, call 911 immediately. Keep all appointments with your doctor and laboratory. Your doctor will order tests to monitor your response to dexamethasone. Regular checkups are especially important for children, as dexamethasone can slow bone growth. If your condition worsens, contact your doctor, as your dose may need adjustment. Carry an identification card indicating that you may require supplemental doses of dexamethasone during periods of stress (e.g., injuries, infections, severe asthma attacks). Ask your doctor or pharmacist how to obtain this card. Include your name, medical conditions, medications and dosages, and your doctor’s contact information on the card. Dexamethasone can make you more susceptible to infections. If you are exposed to chickenpox, measles, or tuberculosis while taking this medication, contact your doctor. Avoid vaccinations, immunizations, or skin tests unless your doctor approves. Report any injuries or signs of infection (e.g., fever, sore throat, pain during urination, muscle aches) during treatment. Your doctor may instruct you to weigh yourself daily and report any unusual weight gain. If your sputum thickens or changes color (e.g., from clear/white to yellow, green, or gray), contact your doctor, as this may indicate an infection. If you have diabetes, dexamethasone may raise your blood sugar levels. Monitor your blood or urine glucose more frequently and contact your doctor if your levels are high or if sugar is present in your urine. Your diabetes medication or diet may need adjustment. Do not share your medication with others. Consult your pharmacist if you have questions about refilling your prescription.
